content: The term Fujian flu refers to influenza caused by specific strains of the Influenza A virus, either the H3N2 subtype (human flu strain) or the H5N1 subtype (avian flu strain). These strains are named after Fujian, a coastal province in China located across the Taiwan Strait from Taiwan. The human H3N2 strain, A/Fujian/411/2002-like, was responsible for an unusually severe flu season in 2003–2004. This severity was attributed to a reassortment event where a minor clade contributed a hemagglutinin gene that became part of the dominant strain during the 2002–2003 flu season. This strain was subsequently included in the trivalent influenza vaccine for the 2004–2005 flu season and remains a common H3N2 strain in humans. The avian H5N1 strain, A/Fujian, is notable for its resistance to standard medical countermeasures and its rapid spread. This variant highlights the ongoing evolution of the H5N1 virus and has been a source of political controversy. Terminology The H5N1 version is often referred to as Fujian-like or Fujian virus, while the H3N2 version is also called Fujian-like. Both are sometimes specified as Type A Fujian flu or A/Fujian flu, with further subtype distinctions such as Fujian Flu (H3N2) or Fujian Flu (H5N1). Full strain names, such as A/Fujian/411/2002-like (H3N2) or Influenza A/Fujian/411/02 (H3N2)-lineage viruses, are also used. A/Fujian (H3N2) During the 2003–2004 flu season, the vaccine was designed to protect against A/Panama (H3N2), A/New Caledonia (H1N1), and B/Hong Kong. However, the emergence of the A/Fujian (H3N2) strain after vaccine production began resulted in only partial protection. Phylogenetic analysis of 156 H3N2 genomes revealed that the appearance of the A/Fujian/411/2002-like strain was due to a significant reassortment event. This event involved a minor clade providing the hemagglutinin gene that later became dominant. By January 2004, A/Fujian/411/2002 (H3N2)-like viruses were the predominant flu strain circulating in Europe. The trivalent influenza vaccine for the 2004–2005 flu season in the United States included A/New Caledonia/20/1999-like (H1N1), A/Fujian/411/2002-like (H3N2), and B/Shanghai/361/2002-like viruses. A/Fujian (H5N1) Specific H5N1 isolates labeled as Fujian include A/Fujian/1/2005 and A/DK/Fujian/1734/05 (or A/Ck/Fujian/1734/2005). The Fujian H5N1 strain is resistant to standard medical countermeasures, spreads rapidly, and demonstrates the ongoing evolution of the H5N1 virus. It has also been a source of political controversy. Researchers have noted that a new H5N1 subtype has become predominant in southern China, possibly due to resistance to poultry vaccines. This strain has been implicated in increased poultry outbreaks and human cases in China. The rise of the Fujian-like strain has been linked to an overall increase in H5N1 infections in live-poultry markets in southern China. Mathematical models suggest that at least 95% of birds need to be protected to prevent silent virus spread, but achieving such high levels of protection is challenging in practice. Resistance to Countermeasures Poultry vaccines are often poorly purified and may contain whole virus particles, leading to suboptimal protection. Vaccines used in poultry are sometimes only vaguely related to circulating flu strains, which can result in incomplete protection. For example, vaccines containing an H5N2 strain isolated in Mexico years ago may not effectively protect against current H5N1 strains. Additionally, poultry vaccines are often weaker than human vaccines, as they are designed to protect chickens for only a short lifespan. Human seasonal flu vaccines contain about 45 micrograms of antigen, while experimental H5N1 vaccines contain 180 micrograms. In contrast, poultry vaccines may contain less than 1 microgram. This discrepancy highlights the challenges of extrapolating data from poultry to humans. H5N1 Evolution The first known strain of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1), A/chicken/Scotland/59, was identified in 1959 but was very different from the current highly pathogenic strain. The dominant HPAI A(H5N1) strain in 2004 evolved from earlier genotypes, creating the Z genotype, also known as Asian lineage HPAI A(H5N1). This genotype emerged through reassortment in 2002 from earlier highly pathogenic genotypes of H5N1 that first appeared in China in 1996 in birds and in Hong Kong in 1997 in humans. H5N1 has mutated through antigenic drift into numerous highly pathogenic varieties, all currently belonging to genotype Z. Asian lineage HPAI A(H5N1) is divided into two antigenic clades. Clade 1 includes human and bird isolates from Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia, while Clade 2 viruses were first identified in China, Indonesia, Japan, and South Korea before spreading westward to the Middle East, Europe, and Africa. Clade 2 viruses have been primarily responsible for human H5N1 infections during late 2005 and 2006. Political Controversy Human disease associated with H5N1 re-emerged in January 2003, marking the first outbreak since 1997. Three individuals in one family were infected after visiting Fujian province in China, with two fatalities. By mid-2003, poultry outbreaks caused by H5N1 occurred in Asia but were not initially recognized as such. Discrepancies between official Chinese government reports and observations on the ground have led to widespread skepticism about China's official H5N1 case numbers. China has been criticized for its handling of H5N1, including the use of substandard vaccines that may mask the virus rather than eliminate it. In response to international pressure, China has shared some H5N1 virus samples with the World Health Organization (WHO) but has been accused of withholding critical information. In late 2006, China provided 20 H5N1 samples from birds and shared significant H5N1 data generated by its laboratories. In May 2007, China shared H5N1 virus samples from humans with the WHO for the first time in nearly a year. Conclusion The Fujian flu, encompassing both H3N2 and H5N1 subtypes, highlights the challenges of influenza virus evolution, vaccine development, and international cooperation in disease control. The rapid spread and resistance of the H5N1 Fujian strain underscore the need for effective vaccines and transparent reporting to mitigate the risk of a potential pandemic.
